blocks.text: Google Sheets on a Mac runs in your browser. I did not find a native Mac app in Google's help pages, so this guide treats Sheets as a browser tab. The keyboard shortcuts come from Google's help page for the computer version. Check them on your own screen before you rely on them.
What marketers do in Google Sheets on a Mac

Marketers mostly use Sheets for three kinds of work: tracking campaigns, building reports, and cleaning data. A lot of that data starts outside Sheets. You export a file from an ad platform or a CRM, open it in the browser, and then fix it. The sheet becomes the place where the numbers get shaped for a meeting.

The research on this is thin. The MarTech and ThoughtSpot findings measure how much time people spend in spreadsheets. They do not list the tasks people do. The task list below reflects common marketing exports and reports. Treat it as a checklist, not a benchmark for your team.

items: Campaign tracking: one row per campaign, with spend, clicks, and conversions by week.
Weekly or monthly reporting: a Summary tab that reads from raw exports.
Data cleanup: fixing names, dates, and duplicate rows before anyone reads the file.
Budget pacing: running totals checked against the plan for the month.
Content calendars: owners, due dates, and status in one table.
Lead lists: importing and de-duplicating contacts from a form or a CRM export.

blocks.text: Why spreadsheets take so much of a marketer's week

In a 2022 MarTech survey of 426 marketers, 77% named spreadsheets as the tool they spend the most time working with. MarTech defined that as 10 or more hours a week. A separate MarTech reader poll, with fewer than 100 respondents, found that almost 80% called spreadsheets a critical marketing tool. Both sources are small and dated. They still show how central the tool is.

A ThoughtSpot survey from October 2022 covered 1,001 office workers in Australia, the UK, and the US. It was not limited to marketers. ThoughtSpot sells analytics software, so read its numbers with that in mind. The same survey also measured friction. 92% of business people said they need to manipulate their spreadsheet data to make it understandable. 40% often struggle to make sense of their data. Manipulating one dataset takes about an hour on average.
Mac keyboard shortcuts for Google Sheets

Google's shortcut page lists these Mac shortcuts for Sheets. ⌘+/ shows the common shortcut list. Option+Shift+K lists every sheet in the file. Option+Up or Option+Down moves between sheets. Option+/ opens the tool finder. Option+Enter opens a hyperlink. The page shows no version number or date, so press ⌘+/ first and confirm the list matches your screen.

blocks.text: Sheet switching saves the most time in a report file. A report usually has a Raw tab, a Clean tab, and a Summary tab. Option+Down and Option+Up walk you through them in order. Option+Shift+K gets you to the right tab when the file has many of them.

blocks.title: If a shortcut does nothing
blocks.text: Check whether a cell is still in edit mode. Press Escape, then try the shortcut again. This is the first thing to check when a shortcut seems to fail.
Set up the file in three tabs

Give every report file the same three tabs. Raw holds exports exactly as they arrived. Clean holds the fixed copy, built with formulas that point at Raw. Summary holds the numbers you show people. This setup keeps one bad import from wiping out a report.

items: Load the export with File > Import, then choose the option that puts it on a new sheet.
Name the tab with the source and the date range, so nobody guesses later.
On Clean, pull values from Raw with formulas such as =Raw!A2, so every fix lives in one place.
On Summary, total the Clean tab with SUMIFS and COUNTIFS, not by hand.
Protect Raw with Data > Protect sheets and ranges, so nobody types over the export.

blocks.text: Formulas for campaign reports

Say column A holds the channel, column B holds the date, and column C holds spend. To total spend for paid social, type =SUMIFS(C:C, A:A, "Paid social"). To count the rows for that channel, type =COUNTIFS(A:A, "Paid social"). The channel name must match the cell text, including any extra spaces.

Lookups fail when a name differs slightly. Wrap the lookup, not the whole sheet. The formula =IFERROR(XLOOKUP(E2, A:A, C:C), "Not found") shows a clear label instead of #N/A. If you wrap the whole report, real errors turn into zeros, and nobody notices. That is the mistake to avoid.

Use QUERY when you want a summary table from Raw without building a pivot by hand. A formula like =QUERY(Raw!A:C, "select A, sum(C) where A is not null group by A", 1) totals spend by channel. Check the output against SUMIFS once. If the two agree, trust the query for the rest of the file.

blocks.title: Fill formulas down
blocks.text: Write the formula once, then fill it down the column. Typing the same formula into each row invites small differences that are hard to spot.
Clean an export before you build a report

Exports arrive messy. Names carry extra spaces. Dates arrive as text, so they sort in the wrong order. The same lead appears twice. Fix these before any formula relies on them. Work on the Clean tab, never on Raw.

items: Trim spaces: select the column, then choose Data > Data cleanup > Trim whitespace.
Remove duplicates: select the rows, then choose Data > Data cleanup > Remove duplicates. Check the row count before you accept.
Split combined fields: select the column, then choose Data > Split text to columns and pick the separator.
Fix dates: select the column, then choose Format > Number and pick a date format. Text dates usually stay left-aligned.
Filter and sort: choose Data > Create a filter, then sort by date or spend.

blocks.text: Menu names change between Sheets versions. If a path does not match your screen, press Option+/ and type the action name. That is faster than hunting through the menu bar.

Check dates after every import. Select the column and look at the alignment. If the values sit on the left, Sheets probably read them as text. Fix that before you sort or sum, or a date filter will miss rows.
Limits that break big marketing sheets

Google says a spreadsheet can hold up to 20 million cells or 100MB. The limit covers the whole file, not one tab. Multiply rows by columns before you import, and leave room for formulas. A file with many raw exports and many formulas grows faster than the export alone suggests.

blocks.text: Connected Sheets follows different rules. Google's product page says it lets you work with billions of rows of BigQuery or Looker data inside the grid. It also lists connections to Asana, HubSpot, Intuit QuickBooks, and Salesforce. The 200k row cap still applies to Connected Sheets pivot tables, so summarize in the query first.
When a file gets slow, split it. Keep the raw exports in their own file. Pull only the columns you need into the report file with IMPORTRANGE. That keeps the report light and the raw data intact.
Gemini in Sheets and the Workspace plan question

Google's product page says Gemini can build or edit a sheet from a prompt, with native formulas, pivot tables, and charts. Sheets canvas can build custom dashboards, heat maps, and Kanban boards without code. Fill with Gemini fills a table at scale from an adjacent table. Gemini also writes and explains formulas, and it fixes formula errors in plain language.

Some of these features need a Workspace plan. Google says some Gemini in Sheets features are only available on Google Workspace plans. Sheets canvas and Fill with Gemini also need the file converted to Google Sheets format first. If an option is missing, check your plan before you blame the file.

blocks.title: Keep the original file
blocks.text: Converting an Excel file changes it. Keep the original .xlsx or CSV before you convert. Google also removes any cell with more than 50,000 characters during conversion.
Mistakes marketers make in Google Sheets

items: Typing over the raw export instead of copying it to a Raw tab first.
Mixing text and numbers in one column, so a total quietly skips rows.
Matching names that have extra spaces or a different spelling of the same channel.
Using whole-column references in many formulas, which makes a large file slow.
Wrapping a whole report in IFERROR, so a broken lookup looks like zero.
Editing a shared formula without checking version history. Use File > Version history > See version history to see who changed what.

blocks.text: Many of these mistakes show up in the summary, not the raw tab. That is why the three-tab setup helps. When a total looks wrong, check Raw first, then Clean, then Summary.
What to ask Lazur while you are in Google Sheets

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘, Option and Command together, and ask about anything on screen. Lazur sees the sheet and answers out loud. It does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you.

items: Where is something: Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.
How do I do this: Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.
Why is this cell wrong: Lazur reads the formula on screen and explains it out loud.
Fill with Gemini or Sheets canvas: Lazur explains what it does and points at the control. You click it.
Draft a note: Lazur writes a short update from the numbers it can see on screen.
Research: Lazur runs it in its own Chrome tabs and returns a summary and a report.

blocks.text: Ask in plain words. "Where is Remove duplicates?" works. So does "Why is this showing zero?" Keep the sheet in front of you, because Lazur answers from what is on screen. Lazur keeps memory of what you asked and did, on your Mac.
Worked example: a #N/A error in a campaign lookup

Your Summary tab shows #N/A in the owner column. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask why. Lazur can read the formula in the formula bar and point at the key column. It explains that the key did not match any row in Raw. You then check the key for extra spaces or a campaign that was renamed in the source. Lazur explains and points. You make the fix.

The same question works for a total that looks too low. Ask Lazur to point at the rows that feed the formula. Then compare those rows with Raw yourself. The quick check often finds the problem, and you learn the pattern for next time.

blocks.title: What Lazur sees
blocks.text: Lazur looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Close any tab with personal or client data before you ask a question about the sheet.
Dictation and drafts for the sheet

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor, in any app. Use it for a cell comment, a note on the Summary tab, or a line in a status email. Snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots help with names you type all the time, such as channel names and campaign codes.
Draft with Lazur when you need words, not formulas. Ask for a two-line update based on the totals on screen. Read it before you send it. Lazur writes the text. You own the numbers and the decision.
Trial, plans, and privacy for Lazur

Lazur has a Pro trial that needs no credit card. It starts the first time you open the app. Pro and Power plans are on the [pricing page](/pricing). Dictation is unlimited on both plans. Get the Mac app from the [download page](/download).

Privacy works like this. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnerships with any app maker.
Where to go next

If your work reaches past spreadsheets, read the [AI assistant for marketers on Mac](/for/marketers) page. For design files, see [Canva for marketers on Mac](/for/marketers/canva). If you plan events, the [Google Sheets guide for event planners](/for/event-planners/google-sheets) covers similar limits.
Start with one raw export. Build the Clean and Summary tabs for that one source. Then add the next source. A small file you trust beats a large file nobody checks.

faq.question: Is there a native Google Sheets app for Mac?
faq.answer: I did not find one in Google's help pages. Those guides cover Sheets in the browser. Open Sheets in your browser, and check Google's help pages for any app option before you assume one exists.

faq.question: Do these Mac shortcuts work in every browser?
faq.answer: I did not test each browser. The shortcut list comes from Google's Sheets Help page for the computer version, which shows no version or date. Press ⌘+/ in your own browser to see the list it shows you.

faq.question: Can Lazur edit my Google Sheet for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It sees the sheet on screen, answers out loud, points at things, and guides you one click at a time. You make every change.

faq.question: Do I need a Google Workspace plan to use Gemini in Sheets?
faq.answer: Some features do. Google says some Gemini in Sheets features are only available on Google Workspace plans. Sheets canvas and Fill with Gemini also need the file converted to Google Sheets format first.

faq.question: How big can a Google Sheets file get?
faq.answer: Google says a spreadsheet can have up to 20 million cells or 100MB. Connected Sheets pivot tables cap at 200k rows, and extracts cap at 500k rows or 5 million cells. Check the limits page before you import a big export.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with Google Sheets in the browser?
faq.answer: Lazur sees your screen in any app, so a Sheets tab in your browser counts. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask. It answers out loud. It does not click or edit for you, and it is not an add-in for Sheets.

faq.question: Does Lazur store my spreadsheet data?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: What does Lazur cost after the trial?
faq.answer: Pro and Power plans are listed on the pricing page. Dictation is unlimited on both plans. The trial needs no credit card and starts the first time you open the app.

faq.question: Does Lazur run on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.
